title: Major Currencies and Correlation
lessons/forex-u2-l1/steps/0/body: **Majors** are the most traded pairs in the world, and they all include the **US dollar**: EUR/USD, USD/JPY, GBP/USD, USD/CHF, AUD/USD, USD/CAD and NZD/USD. High liquidity usually means a **tighter spread**.
lessons/forex-u2-l1/steps/0/tip: Most beginners start with the majors: costs are lower, and there's more analysis and news available.
lessons/forex-u2-l1/steps/1/prompt: Which one is a major pair?
lessons/forex-u2-l1/steps/1/explanation: USD/CAD pairs the US dollar with a major currency (the Canadian dollar). EUR/GBP and GBP/JPY have no dollar (minors), and USD/TRY is an exotic.
lessons/forex-u2-l1/steps/2/body: A **minor**, or **cross**, is two major currencies **without the dollar**, like EUR/GBP and GBP/JPY. An **exotic** pairs a major currency with the currency of an **emerging or smaller economy**, like USD/TRY (Turkish lira) or USD/ZAR (South African rand).
lessons/forex-u2-l1/steps/4/statement: EUR/GBP is a major pair, because both of its currencies are major currencies.
lessons/forex-u2-l1/steps/4/explanation: Majors always include the US dollar. EUR/GBP is two majors without the dollar, so it's a minor (cross).
lessons/forex-u2-l1/steps/5/body: The further you move from majors toward exotics, the **lower the liquidity**: **wider spreads**, more sudden jumps and usually **heavier swaps**, because these countries' interest rates are far from those of the major currencies.
lessons/forex-u2-l1/steps/5/example/rows: Spread can be tens of pips or more
lessons/forex-u2-l1/steps/6/prompt: You have a small account and want to take lots of short-term trades. Which pair makes the most sense cost-wise?
lessons/forex-u2-l1/steps/6/explanation: In short trades, the spread eats a big chunk of your profit. EUR/USD is the most liquid pair and usually has the tightest spread.
lessons/forex-u2-l1/steps/7/sentence: Pairs made of two major currencies without the dollar are called ___ pairs, and pairs with an emerging-economy currency are called ___ pairs.
lessons/forex-u2-l1/steps/7/explanation: Major = dollar + a major currency, minor = two majors without the dollar, exotic = a major + an emerging-market currency.
lessons/forex-u2-l2/title: Currency personalities: USD, JPY, CHF, AUD…
lessons/forex-u2-l2/steps/0/body: The **dollar** is the world's main reserve currency. Decisions by the **Federal Reserve (Fed)** and data like **inflation (CPI)** and **jobs (NFP)** move almost every pair. In global crises, demand for dollars **often** rises too.
lessons/forex-u2-l2/steps/1/body: When fear hits the market (**risk-off**), money usually flows into **safe** currencies like the **Japanese yen (JPY)** and the **Swiss franc (CHF)**, and they get stronger. This has repeated for years, though it's not a permanent rule.
lessons/forex-u2-l2/steps/2/prompt: A global financial crisis has started and markets are scared. Which currency will probably see more demand?
lessons/forex-u2-l2/steps/2/explanation: In risk-off, money flows to safe havens like the yen and franc. Commodity and emerging-market currencies usually weaken.
lessons/forex-u2-l2/steps/3/title: Commodity currencies: AUD, NZD and CAD
lessons/forex-u2-l2/steps/3/body: These economies depend on **commodity exports**: the **Australian dollar** on iron ore, metals and demand from **China**, the **New Zealand dollar** on dairy and farming, and the **Canadian dollar** on **oil**. When risk appetite is high (**risk-on**), AUD and NZD are usually stronger.
lessons/forex-u2-l2/steps/5/prompt: Oil prices have jumped, and USD/CAD has just broken below support at 1.3600. What's more likely for the next candle?
lessons/forex-u2-l2/steps/5/explanation: Pricier oil usually strengthens the Canadian dollar, so USD/CAD falls. A strong candle breaking support confirms it. But the oil–CAD link isn't guaranteed, so you still need a stop loss.
lessons/forex-u2-l2/steps/6/statement: The Australian dollar usually gets stronger when the market is scared (risk-off).
lessons/forex-u2-l2/steps/6/explanation: AUD is a risky commodity currency. When the market is scared it usually weakens, and money flows to the yen, franc and dollar.
lessons/forex-u2-l2/steps/7/prompt: AUD/JPY has kept climbing on the daily chart. Which market mood fits this move best?
lessons/forex-u2-l2/steps/7/explanation: AUD is a risky currency and JPY is a safe haven. A rising AUD/JPY means money has moved from safety into risk. That's why many traders use this pair as a risk-appetite thermometer.
lessons/forex-u2-l2/steps/8/sentence: When fear rules the market, safe-haven currencies like the ___ and the Swiss franc usually get ___.
lessons/forex-u2-l2/steps/8/explanation: In risk-off, money hides in safe havens like the yen and franc, while risky currencies like AUD and NZD usually weaken.
lessons/forex-u2-l3/steps/0/body: **Correlation** shows how similarly two pairs move. It ranges from **-1 to +1**. Near **+1** means they move almost together, near **-1** means almost opposite, and near **0** means there's no real link.
lessons/forex-u2-l3/steps/1/body: **EUR/USD and GBP/USD** usually have a strong positive correlation, since both are priced against the dollar. **EUR/USD and USD/CHF** usually have a strong negative correlation, because the dollar is second in one and first in the other. **AUD/USD and NZD/USD** usually move like twins too.
lessons/forex-u2-l3/steps/1/tip: Correlation isn't fixed. It shifts with economic conditions, so check it every now and then.
lessons/forex-u2-l3/steps/2/prompt: What correlation do EUR/USD and USD/CHF usually have?
lessons/forex-u2-l3/steps/2/explanation: In EUR/USD the dollar is the second currency; in USD/CHF it's the first. When the dollar weakens, the first usually rises and the second falls.
lessons/forex-u2-l3/steps/3/statement: The correlation between currency pairs is fixed and never changes.
lessons/forex-u2-l3/steps/3/explanation: Correlation shifts with interest rates, news and market mood, and sometimes even disappears for a while. You need to check it regularly.
lessons/forex-u2-l3/steps/4/body: If you buy **EUR/USD and GBP/USD** at the same time, you've really bet **twice on a weaker dollar**. If the dollar gets stronger, **both** usually lose. Your real risk is close to double.
lessons/forex-u2-l3/steps/5/prompt: The dollar is under pressure everywhere after a weak report, and EUR/USD has just broken its previous high. This is the GBP/USD chart. What's more likely?
lessons/forex-u2-l3/steps/5/explanation: GBP/USD usually has a strong positive correlation with EUR/USD, and a weak dollar lifts both. The last strong candle also broke the previous high. But correlation isn't a guarantee, so you still need a stop loss.
lessons/forex-u2-l3/steps/6/prompt: EUR/USD was rising over the same period. Which relationship fits this USD/CHF chart?
lessons/forex-u2-l3/steps/6/explanation: EUR/USD went up and USD/CHF went down, so they moved in opposite directions. That's the well-known negative correlation between these two pairs.
lessons/forex-u2-l3/steps/7/prompt: You bought EUR/USD. Now you see a buy signal on USD/CHF too. What happens if you open both?
lessons/forex-u2-l3/steps/7/options/0: They largely cancel each other out
lessons/forex-u2-l3/steps/7/options/2: Two signals are sure to double your profit
lessons/forex-u2-l3/steps/7/options/3: These two pairs have no effect on each other
lessons/forex-u2-l3/steps/7/explanation: Buying EUR/USD means selling dollars, and buying USD/CHF means buying dollars. With a strong negative correlation, the gain on one is usually canceled by the loss on the other, and you just pay costs twice.
lessons/forex-u2-l3/steps/8/sentence: If two pairs have a correlation near ___, they usually move together; near ___, they move in opposite directions.
lessons/forex-u2-l3/steps/8/explanation: Correlation runs from -1 to +1: +1 means together, -1 means opposite, and 0 means no link.
